nature-nbs-327.title: Point-of-use water treatment: cleaning water at home
nature-nbs-327.text: The last place to make water safe is the place where it is drunk. Point-of-use water treatment cleans drinking water at the household or community scale, right where people use it. How much disease it prevents depends on two things: how well it removes pathogens when used properly, and social factors such as ease of use and cultural acceptability. Technologies can deliver more or less health benefit than lab removal suggests. Proponents therefore put the priority on reaching many low-income households in a way that lasts.

nature-nbs-328.title: Water fluoridation: a contested addition to public water
nature-nbs-328.text: Some public water supplies have something deliberately added to them. Water fluoridation is the controlled addition of fluoride to reduce tooth decay. Many areas add it at low concentrations, below 1.0 ppm, to improve dental health. The dose matters, because in large amounts fluoride interferes with bone formation. Fluoridation also remains controversial in some communities, so the practice is not accepted everywhere.

nature-nbs-321.title: Dam spillways and outlets: how a reservoir lets water go
nature-nbs-321.text: A dam that can only hold water is a dam that can fail. Spillways and outlets are the auxiliary structures that release water from a reservoir. Spillways pass excess flow in a controlled way, so heavy rain upstream does not overtop the dam and risk its failure. Outlets, usually low in the dam, let operators lower the reservoir. They do so for maintenance, flushing sediment, hydropower, dry-season flow downstream or to reduce stress on the structure.

nature-nbs-320.title: Dam types: embankment, gravity, buttress and arch
nature-nbs-320.text: Dams are grouped by how their structure holds back water. Embankment dams, the most common type, are compacted mounds of earth or rock, classed as earthfill or rockfill. Gravity dams resist the water upstream with their own weight and are now nearly all concrete. Buttress dams have an inclined upstream face propped by triangular buttresses. An arch dam is a curved concrete structure that passes the water's force horizontally into the valley walls. Gravity and buttress dams pass it down into the foundation instead.

nature-nbs-333.title: How levees change rivers, floodplains and habitat
nature-nbs-333.text: A levee protects the land behind it, but it also cuts the river off from that land. Levees constrain flood pulses and the deposition of nutrients, organic material and sediment on floodplains and wetlands. Less overbank deposition can bring coastal erosion and land loss downstream. The reverse is also seen: where levees were removed, riparian habitat and biodiversity increased.

nature-nbs-332.title: Levee failure: how the wall gives way
nature-nbs-332.text: A levee is only as good as its worst hour. Failure causes include overtopping, erosion, structural failure and saturation of the levee itself. A breach is the most frequent and dangerous. It can leave a fan-shaped sediment deposit called a crevasse splay. If the river is permanently diverted through the gap, the breach can become a meander cutoff. The 2005 levee failures in Greater New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina were a catastrophic example.

nature-nbs-331.title: Natural levees: ridges rivers build themselves
nature-nbs-331.text: Rivers raise their own banks. A natural levee is a ridge of mud and silt that forms on a floodplain beside a channel without human help. As flood water loses velocity, the coarser load drops next to the channel and finer sediment settles farther out. Over many floods the ridge builds up. The process can turn against the land: if the channel keeps aggrading, overtopping becomes likely again. The bed can even rise above the floodplain, as with the Yellow River near the sea.

nature-nbs-324.title: Ending combined sewer overflows: separation, storage and green fixes
nature-nbs-324.text: Cities have several ways to stop untreated overflows. Sewer separation builds a second pipe system, but cities often manage only part of it because of cost or physical limits. Washington, D.C. separated four small neighbourhoods in 2011 for $11 million. Storage tunnels hold combined flow from many outfalls without treating it, then pump it to a treatment plant after the storm. Sharing capacity reduces the total storage needed. Other measures add treatment capacity or green infrastructure. Litigation in 2002 forced Toledo, Ohio, to double treatment capacity and build a storage basin to end most overflows.

nature-nbs-312.title: Longshore drift: how waves move a beach sideways
nature-nbs-312.text:
A beach is never still, even when it looks it. Longshore drift is the transport of sediment (clay, silt, pebbles, sand, shingle, shells) along a coast, parallel to the shoreline. It depends on the angle of the incoming waves.

Two things move the sand. Oblique incoming wind squeezes water along the coast and creates a current parallel to it. The sediment this current carries within the surf zone is longshore drift. Breaking surf also sends water up the beach at an angle, called swash, and gravity drains it straight downslope as backwash. That zigzag moves beach sand too.

The first scientific studies of coastal sediment movement began in the mid-1800s, before the term existed. Early 20th-century oceanographers and coastal engineers found the angle of wave approach paramount. That led to the longshore current concept and the drift-aligned beach, with deposition on one side and erosion on the other. The balance is delicate: a slight change in sediment supply or wind direction can change drift dramatically, altering how a beach forms and evolves.

nature-nbs-315.title: Detached breakwaters: offshore walls that build beaches
nature-nbs-315.text: Some shore protection stands apart from the shore. A detached breakwater is built to build up sandy material between it and the coast. It has no connection to the shoreline, so currents and sediment can pass between structure and shore, which accommodates storm drawdown. Behind it lies a zone of reduced wave energy, and this encourages sand deposition on its lee side.

nature-nbs-316.title: How ports and harbours disrupt longshore drift
nature-nbs-316.text: A harbor wall is a dam for sand. Ports and harbours can seriously disrupt natural longshore drift by altering sedimentation patterns. The altered pattern can cause accretion or erosion of a beach or coastal system, and it threatens longer-term shoreline evolution. At Timaru, New Zealand, the late 19th-century port blocked coarse sediment drifting north. The sediment accreted south of the port instead, at South beach.

nature-nbs-313.title: Sediment budgets: the bookkeeping of a coastline
nature-nbs-313.text: A coast gains and loses sand like an account. A sediment budget tallies the sources and sinks within a coastal system. Sediment from any source enters the system and is carried along by longshore drift. Artificial sinks include mining or extraction. Inlet ebb-tidal shoals show budget and drift working together, since they store sand moved by longshore transport.

nature-nbs-314.title: Spits and barriers: landforms built by drifting sand
nature-nbs-314.text: Where drift deposits sediment, land can grow out into the sea. A spit is attached to land at one end; a barrier is attached at both. A spit forms where drift passes a point, such as a river mouth, at which the dominant drift direction and the shoreline do not veer the same way. Its distal end is detached and may hook. Barrier systems may enclose an estuary or lagoon, as the Kaitorete Spit does for Lake Ellesmere / Te Waihora. Tidal inlets on drift shores accumulate sediment in flood and ebb shoals and act as sinks and sources. An unstructured inlet lets sediment by-pass and form bars down-drift.

nature-nbs-347.title: Ecology: the science of organisms and their surroundings
nature-nbs-347.text:
Pull one thread in a living system and the effects may spread far beyond it. Ecology is the natural science that studies the interactions between organisms and their environments. It considers organisms at community, ecosystem and biosphere levels. It overlaps with biogeography, evolutionary biology, genetics and ethology.

Ecology is both a biological science and a human science. It is also an applied science of restoration, used to repair disturbed sites. A disturbance is any process that changes or removes biomass from a community, such as fire, flood, drought or predation.

The structure of an ecosystem is nonlinear. Small changes to critical variables, such as the number of nitrogen fixers, can cause disproportionate and perhaps irreversible changes. Ecologists also study nutrient budgets, and they have found a global feedback between ecosystems and planetary physical parameters such as soil, pH, water and atmospheric gases.

nature-nbs-350.title: Pasture: land set aside for grazing
nature-nbs-350.text: Pasture is land used for grazing. In the narrow sense it is enclosed farmland grazed by domesticated livestock, with forage mostly of grasses plus legumes and forbs. Meadow is ungrazed, or grazed only after mowing for hay, whereas pasture is typically grazed through the summer. It differs from rangeland by intensive practices of seeding, irrigation and fertilizer. Rangelands grow mainly native vegetation under extensive management such as controlled burning and regulated grazing. For ruminants, pasture rather than trough-feeding is the main food source, and it dominates where terrain makes cropping difficult, as in arid or mountainous regions. Over generations, tending and fertilizing by grazers can make a pasture and its ruminants integral to a particular ecosystem.

nature-nbs-342.title: Tillage: turning the soil for crops
nature-nbs-342.text:
Farmers have been stirring soil for a very long time. The earliest evidence of plough use dates to around 4000 BCE in Mesopotamia. Tillage is the agricultural preparation of soil by mechanical agitation such as digging, stirring and overturning. It can be done with hand tools, or with draft-animal and mechanized work such as ploughing, harrowing, rototilling and cultivating.

The benefits are real. Tillage loosens and aerates topsoil and mixes residue, organic matter and nutrients evenly into it. The costs are real too. They include nutrient and water-storage loss, lower infiltration and more runoff, and erosion from dislodged soil particles.

Tilling can also damage archaeology. English Heritage said in 2003 that modern tractor ploughing had done as much damage in six decades as traditional farming in six centuries. One alternative is {{ref:nature-nbs-290}}, which grows crops for years without tillage, using herbicides, compaction-tolerant varieties and seeding equipment. It cuts erosion and diesel use.
